articles.title: The pet I’ll never forget: Poppy the curious, clever dog – who searches for missing people
articles.summary: A beloved family pet, she is also the best employee ever, brilliant at her rescue work. If everyone could be more like Poppy, the world would be a better place. When we picked up a nine-week-old black labrador from a couple just outside Callander, Scotland, I had no idea that she would soon be an…
body: Poppy and our team of dogs look for missing people. My colleagues and I then provide any medical assistance needed. She is trained to search without needing to smell someone’s scent from an item such as clothing. During training, we hide our volunteers along the riverbank, in the woods, beside lochs and canals, and set the dogs off. They have to find the people and come back. Poppy’s curious nature has served her well. She loves the undergrowth, sniffing about and finding things.

She has been involved in a couple of searches, including one for a missing army veteran in the Scottish Borders, which, unfortunately, turned into a body recovery. She was also tasked with going up to Inverness to help find a missing child in the woods who, thankfully, was found by the police.
Poppy is the best employee. When she has her search jacket on, she knows she is going to look for people and the difference is apparent: she changes from family pet mode to working dog mode.

articles.title: Is your partner on their phone and ignoring you? I’ve got a buzzword for that
articles.summary: From microcheating to quiet quitting to weaponised incompetence, new terms to describe relationship failings are abundant. But that doesn’t mean there’s not space for some more... Are you committing “attention infidelity”?
body: A re you committing “attention infidelity”? The New York Times alerted me to this expression, coined by the public opinion researcher Daniel Cox in a new book on the “crisis of human connection”. It’s exactly what you’d expect: failing to focus fully on your partner because you’re indulging in what the NYT calls, rather judgily, “the banal distraction of dead-eyed scrolling”. Who are you calling dead-eyed? This reel of an armadillo in a paddling pool has my animated attention!

Surely we’re all a bit attention-unfaithful – only saints don’t sometimes absent-mindedly thumb through medieval manuscript hedgehog memes while their partner relates a boring anecdote about how they thought they saw a strange bird that turned out to be a plastic bag. What I find more interesting is how we seem now to need a lexicon of relationship bad behaviour.
points: From microcheating to quiet quitting to weaponised incompetence, new terms to describe relationship failings are abundant.

articles.title: Karl review – straightforward tribute tells inside story of fashion world’s great eccentric Karl Lagerfeld
articles.summary: Based on Lagerfeld’s biography, director Nick Hooker gets access to the designer’s inner circle, but ultimately fails to find the man behind the high collar and sunglasses.
body: Karl Lagerfeld had never set foot inside a supermarket before he had one built on a catwalk in 2014, featuring models browsing aisles with baskets shopping for Chanel-branded fromage. It was classic Lagerfeld: very silly but a stroke of genius. The fashion designer was easy to poke fun at, with his white bouffant-plus-ponytail hairstyle and black leather gloves. But behind the persona was a man who spoke four languages fluently, a workaholic still running Chanel, Fendi and his own label Karl Lagerfeld into his 80s.

This dutiful, uncontroversial documentary is based on William Middleton’s biography Paradise Now: The Extraordinary Life of Karl Lagerfeld. As well as archive footage of Lagerfeld, film-maker Nick Hooker gets access to the designer’s inner circle, but ultimately his documentary fails to chip away at the persona. (This is no criticism: I once interviewed Lagerfeld, a frustrating 30 minutes during which the dark glasses stayed on and he answered questions with bon mot witticisms but gave nothing away.) In a clip at the start of the film, Lagerfeld admits that he has spent so long performing a role that not even those closest to him really know who he is.
points: Based on Lagerfeld’s biography, director Nick Hooker gets access to the designer’s inner circle, but ultimately fails to find the man behind the high collar and sunglasses.

articles.title: Is it true that … houseplants freshen the air in our homes and offices?
articles.summary: If you want to seriously oxygenate your rooms with greenery, you’re going to need a lot of space. ‘Plants take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen when they photosynthesise,” says John Tregoning, a professor at Imperial College London and author of Live Forever?
body: It’s tempting to think of plants as a kind of natural air filter, cleaning the air in stuffy, poorly ventilated spaces. But the reality is different.

The average plant produces just a few litres of oxygen a day. A person, by comparison, consumes about 500 litres. So, to produce enough oxygen for one person, you’d need hundreds of plants. “Quite a mad number of plants to have in a room,” says Tregoning. You would also need plenty of light for photosynthesis to take place.
Tregoning points out that we shouldn’t look to keep increasing the oxygen level indoors infinitely: “It’s quite poisonous at high levels.”

He says people are right to think about air quality in their homes and offices. “Higher levels of carbon dioxide are going to make you feel a bit groggy. If you’re working with lots of other people, poor ventilation is also going to lead to faster transmission of colds and illnesses.”

articles.title: Pumpkin Bolognese
articles.summary: Canned purée delivers rich body and deep flavor, without the nonna-level cook time.
body: This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 1 large white or yellow onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. freshly grated nutmeg and stir to combine. Cover pot and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are very soft, 8–10 minutes. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are golden around the edges, about 5 minutes.

Uncover pot and add 1 lb. ground beef, preferably 20% fat; season lightly with salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until beef is very lightly browned but not crisp (it will still be pink in spots), 6–8 minutes. Pour in 1 cup whole milk and cook, stirring occasionally, until milk has evaporated and fat is pooling on surface of meat, 7–10 minutes.
points: Canned purée delivers rich body and deep flavor, without the nonna-level cook time.

articles.title: 5 All-New Recipes for Pumpkin Week
articles.summary: The fluffiest focaccia, cream cheese-stuffed muffins, Sunday bolognese, and more ways we’re cooking with canned pumpkin in 2026.
body: Pumpkin is more than just a canvas to highlight cinnamon and nutmeg. This autumn staple has a vegetally sweet and nutty flavor that only intensifies as it cooks. That’s why classic pumpkin pie and pumpkin bread are so good. But it’s also why this ingredient has such a wide range. Canned purée ( please don’t make your own ) lends moisture and buttery smoothness to sauces and batters alike. So we’re back again this year, sharing five brand new—and extremely delicious—recipes.

There’s a fluffy pumpkin focaccia with a wide-open crumb. Cheesy enchiladas with a lick of mild heat. Tender muffins stuffed with tangy cream cheese. Sunday-worthy bolognese and a three-ingredient (!) soup that tastes like it simmered all day long. They’re all anything but basic.

Pumpkin certainly belongs on the dessert table, but it deserves a place on the dinner table too. With Pumpkin Week, you can do both. Don’t forget to tag us on social @bonappetitmag when you show off your dish!
The plush and crisp bread we know and love is ripe for the pumpkin treatment, lending it a golden hue and earthy sweetness.
points: The fluffiest focaccia, cream cheese-stuffed muffins, Sunday bolognese, and more ways we’re cooking with canned pumpkin in 2026.

articles.title: 28 Best Beach Wedding Dresses for a Walk Down a Sandy Aisle
articles.summary: Read on to discover tips for finding the best beach wedding dress—plus, shop 28 of our favorite designs here.
body: Couples don’t choose seaside nuptials by accident. Some are drawn to the panoramic views, others love being near the water, and most want a celebration that feels more like a getaway than a formal affair. A beach wedding dress, then, should feel special enough for the occasion while still letting the scenery take the lead.

A quick word of advice: Some silhouettes don’t belong on the beach. A dramatic ball gown may be tempting, but a rigid, voluminous skirt can make crossing sand unnecessarily difficult. Heavy fabrics will also leave you overheated before the vows (though you could make a case for embellishments, so long as they’re restrained), while ultra-delicate materials risk snagging on a stray shell—or being ruined by a splash of saltwater.

Though coastal bridal ensembles tend to be less formal, options still range from barely-there slips to full-length numbers—and the best of them share one quality: fabrics that move. Think silk, chiffon, crepe, and organza, all of which catch the wind and photograph beautifully against a shoreside backdrop.

articles.title: Frasers Group CEO Michael Murray on Matches, His Plans for Harvey Nichols and His Intentions for Hugo Boss
articles.summary: Frasers Group is hosting its first-ever event in Paris during Fashion Week. As the group continues to elevate its positioning with luxury retail and brand acquisitions, Murray sat down with Vogue Business to elucidate his strategy.
body: Tonight, at a luxury hotel in the 8th arrondissement, Frasers Group CEO Michael Murray is hosting a cocktail party during Paris Fashion Week. The event will celebrate Frasers Group Luxury, a new division of the business comprising Flannels, The Webster, and recently acquired British department store Harvey Nichols. The portfolio also includes Boss, which Frasers is hoping to acquire: the group just upped its stake to 47.89% in August, and Murray was recently made chairman of the board.

It’s the first time Frasers has held a luxury event during Paris Fashion Week, but as the group continues with brand acquisitions, Murray is keen to underline its elevated positioning. The 500-strong guestlist, he says, will include leading luxury CEOs who partner with Frasers across its retail portfolio, franchisees and partners from across Europe, and industry insiders in town for Paris Fashion Week.
points: Frasers Group is hosting its first-ever event in Paris during Fashion Week.

articles.title: India’s Gaurav Gupta Is Betting on a Permanent Paris Address
articles.summary: The designer opened his by-appointment couture atelier on October 2, putting his own revenue behind a permanent Paris outpost as global demand grows.
body: While India’s growing crop of global fashion brands are absent from the Paris Fashion Week schedule this season, Gaurav Gupta is using the moment to highlight a different milestone. Nestled in the city’s 8th arrondissement, the Delhi-born designer’s new by-appointment couture atelier, which sits just two minutes from the Grand Palais, soft-launched on October 2.

While Gupta is a returning fixture on the Paris calendar, ever since his debut in 2023 at Palais de Tokyo, the opening marks his presence in the fashion capital not just during the week, but permanently. Fellow Indian couturier Vaishali S opened a location on Boulevard Saint-Germain in 2024, Sabyasachi and Anita Dongre have stores in New York, and Manish Malhotra has one in Dubai. But Gupta has taken an alternative approach: no shopfront and no footfall to chase.
points: The designer opened his by-appointment couture atelier on October 2, putting his own revenue behind a permanent Paris outpost as global demand grows.

articles.title: No-Knead Pumpkin Focaccia
body: This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Mix one ¼-oz. envelope active dry yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), 5 cups (625 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1½ cups warm water in a large bowl until a dry, shaggy dough forms. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot 15 minutes.

Place a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough and moisten hands in water, shaking off excess. Stretch 1 side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat process 3 more times, turning bowl after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Remoisten your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat entire process 2 more times (folding and resting), about 1 hour more. By the last full fold, the dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

articles.title: Does Beauty Need to Reinvest in Innovation?
articles.summary: The simultaneous launch of near-identical eye patch products from Fenty Beauty, Huda Beauty, and Glow Recipe prompted an existential crisis for the industry.
body: Last week, Fenty, Glow Recipe, and Huda Beauty announced near-identical product launches within days of one another: undereye masks presented in the same container with a novel packaging mechanism that slices a fresh eye patch when dispensed. The coincidence sparked an uproar on social media, quickly dubbed “Eye Patch Gate”.

While the brands poked fun at the coincidence on social media, it seemed to confirm what many suspected happened behind the scenes of the beauty industry: that brands touting product innovation order packaging, ingredients and even formulas from the same manufacturers but put their label over it.

Consumers today are savvier and more knowledgeable than ever before, and they are increasingly demanding. They want to see meaningful results, and they understand value. Unstable geopolitical conditions and unceasing inflation has them sharper, more on edge, more likely to turn on a brand they feel isn’t acting authentically or in their best interests. Consumers are becoming more attuned to, and fatigued by, the frenetic pace of new product launches. Terms like “deinfluencing” and “underconsumption core” are trending on TikTok.
